title: Molecular Biology and Nutritional Biochemistry
description: DNA replication, transcription, translation and gene regulation, recombinant DNA technology, and the biochemistry of nutrition and trace elements.

topics.title: DNA Replication and Repair
topics.summary: Semi-conservative replication, enzymes of replication, telomeres and DNA repair.

notes.b: DNA replication is semi-conservative (Meselson and Stahl): each new double helix contains one parental and one new strand. It begins at origins of replication; helicase unwinds the helix, single-strand binding proteins stabilise it, topoisomerases relieve supercoiling (bacterial DNA gyrase is the target of fluoroquinolones), primase lays down RNA primers, and DNA polymerase synthesises new DNA only in the 5′→3′ direction. The leading strand is made continuously; the lagging strand is made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase. DNA polymerases proofread (3′→5′ exonuclease). Telomerase (a reverse transcriptase) maintains chromosome ends in germ cells, stem cells and most cancers.

Repair pathways include mismatch repair (defective in hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, Lynch syndrome), base excision repair, nucleotide excision repair (removes UV-induced thymine dimers — defective in xeroderma pigmentosum, causing extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancers) and double-strand break repair by homologous recombination (BRCA1/BRCA2) or non-homologous end joining. The tumour suppressor p53 ('guardian of the genome') halts the cell cycle for repair or triggers apoptosis.
k: Xeroderma pigmentosum: nucleotide excision repair defect

topics.title: Transcription and RNA Processing
topics.summary: RNA polymerases, promoters, mRNA processing, and inhibitors of transcription.

notes.b: Transcription copies a DNA template strand into RNA (5′→3′) using RNA polymerase, which needs no primer. In eukaryotes, RNA polymerase I makes most rRNA, polymerase II makes mRNA (inhibited by α-amanitin from Amanita mushrooms), and polymerase III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA. Transcription begins at promoters (e.g. the TATA box) with the help of transcription factors, and enhancers can increase it from a distance. Bacteria have a single RNA polymerase (inhibited by rifampicin) with a sigma factor that recognises promoters.
k: RNA pol II makes mRNA; α-amanitin inhibits it

notes.b: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed in the nucleus: a 7-methylguanosine cap is added at the 5′ end, a poly-A tail at the 3′ end, and introns are removed by the spliceosome (snRNPs), joining exons. Alternative splicing lets one gene encode several proteins. Mutations at splice sites cause some β-thalassaemias. Autoantibodies to snRNPs (anti-Smith) are specific for systemic lupus erythematosus. Mature mRNA is exported to the cytoplasm for translation.
k: Alternative splicing: one gene → many proteins

topics.title: Translation and the Genetic Code
topics.summary: Codons, tRNA and ribosomes, steps of protein synthesis, antibiotics and post-translational modification.

notes.b: The genetic code is a triplet code read 5′→3′ on mRNA; it is degenerate (most amino acids have several codons), non-overlapping, unambiguous and almost universal. AUG (methionine) is the start codon; UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons. tRNAs carry amino acids attached by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and recognise codons via anticodons (wobble at the third base). Translation on ribosomes (eukaryotic 80S = 60S + 40S; prokaryotic 70S = 50S + 30S) has initiation, elongation (peptide bond formation by peptidyl transferase, an rRNA ribozyme) and termination (release factors at stop codons).
k: AUG start; UAA, UAG, UGA stop
Code is degenerate and nearly universal

notes.b: Many antibiotics selectively target bacterial 70S ribosomes: aminoglycosides (gentamicin) and tetracyclines bind the 30S subunit; macrolides (erythromycin, azithromycin), chloramphenicol, clindamycin and linezolid bind the 50S subunit. Diphtheria toxin inactivates eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (EF-2). After translation, proteins may be folded by chaperones, glycosylated, phosphorylated, cleaved (proinsulin → insulin + C-peptide), or targeted by signal sequences to the ER. Collagen requires vitamin C-dependent hydroxylation of proline and lysine.

topics.title: Gene Regulation and Recombinant DNA Technology
topics.summary: The lac operon, epigenetics, recombinant DNA, cloning and biotechnology in medicine.

notes.b: In bacteria, genes are organised into operons. The lac operon (Jacob and Monod) is inducible: the repressor binds the operator in the absence of lactose; allolactose inactivates the repressor, and high expression also needs low glucose (cAMP–CAP positive control). The trp operon is repressible. In eukaryotes, regulation occurs at chromatin (histone acetylation opens chromatin and increases transcription; DNA methylation at CpG islands silences genes), transcription factors, RNA processing, microRNAs and protein modification. Genomic imprinting (e.g. Prader–Willi and Angelman syndromes) is an epigenetic effect.
k: Lac operon: inducible, needs lactose and low glucose

notes.b: Recombinant DNA technology uses restriction enzymes (cutting at palindromic sites, often leaving sticky ends), DNA ligase, and vectors (plasmids, bacteriophages, viral vectors) to insert genes into host cells. cDNA made from mRNA by reverse transcriptase lacks introns and can be expressed in bacteria. Applications: recombinant human insulin, growth hormone, erythropoietin, hepatitis B surface antigen vaccine, monoclonal antibodies, gene therapy, and CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing. Real-time (quantitative) PCR measures viral load (HIV) and GeneXpert MTB/RIF detects TB and rifampicin resistance.
k: cDNA from mRNA via reverse transcriptase
GeneXpert detects TB and rifampicin resistance

topics.title: Nutritional Biochemistry and Trace Elements
topics.summary: Energy requirements, macronutrients, protein quality, minerals and trace elements.

notes.b: Energy yields: carbohydrate and protein 4 kcal/g (17 kJ/g), fat 9 kcal/g (37 kJ/g), alcohol 7 kcal/g. Total energy expenditure = basal metabolic rate (about 60–70%) + thermic effect of food (~10%) + physical activity. Body mass index = weight (kg)/height (m)²: normal 18.5–24.9, overweight 25–29.9, obese ≥ 30. Protein quality depends on essential amino acid content; cereals are low in lysine and legumes low in methionine, so combining them (e.g. rice and beans, a common Nigerian meal) gives complementary proteins. Nitrogen balance is positive in growth, pregnancy and recovery, negative in starvation, burns and severe illness.

Iron: absorbed as Fe2+ in the duodenum (enhanced by vitamin C, reduced by phytates and tannins in tea); stored as ferritin; deficiency causes microcytic anaemia — the commonest nutritional deficiency worldwide. Iodine: thyroid hormones; deficiency causes goitre and cretinism. Zinc: cofactor for many enzymes; deficiency causes growth retardation, poor wound healing, acrodermatitis and diarrhoea — zinc supplements are given with ORS for childhood diarrhoea. Calcium and vitamin D: bone health. Fluoride prevents dental caries but excess causes fluorosis. Selenium is part of glutathione peroxidase. Copper deficiency causes anaemia; Wilson disease is copper overload.
k: Iron absorbed as Fe2+; vitamin C helps
